meta.name: J. H. Macmahon
meta.source: Hippolytus, The Refutation of All Heresies (Philosophumena), translated by J. H. Macmahon, in the Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. V (1886): the hymn of the Naassenes, Refutation V.5 (the Naassene Psalm); Wikisource transcription
meta.note: The chapters keep the numbers of the translation; a verse is a paragraph of the chapter. Hippolytus reports the doctrines of the heresies, often in their own words.

5.1: The foregoing remarks, then, though few out of many, we have thought proper to bring forward. For innumerable are the silly and crazy attempts of folly. But since, to the best of our ability, we have explained the unknown Gnosis, it seemed expedient likewise to adduce the following point. This psalm of theirs has been composed, by which they seem to celebrate all the mysteries of the error (advanced by) them in a hymn, couched in the following terms:—
5.2: The world’s producing law was Primal Mind,
5.3: And next was First-born’s outpoured Chaos;
5.4: And third, the soul received its law of toil:
5.5: Encircl’d, therefore, with an aqueous form,
5.6: With care o’erpowered it succumbs to death.
5.7: Now holding sway, it eyes the light,
5.8: And now it weeps on misery flung;
5.9: Now it mourns, now it thrills with joy;
5.10: Now it wails, now it hears its doom;
5.11: Now it hears its doom, now it dies,
5.12: And now it leaves us, never to return.
5.13: It, hapless straying, treads the maze of ills.
5.15: A strife of ills across the earth
5.17: But bitter Chaos (man) seeks to shun,
5.18: And knows not how to pass it through.
5.19: On this account, O Father, send me;
5.23: And forms of Gods I’ll show;
5.24: And secrets of the saintly path,

naassene.5: Explanation of the System of the Naasseni Taken from One of Their Hymns.
